question: How does Debussy make a large arrival out of many small changes in motion and colour?
intro: Low strings, harps and timpani begin before a clear horizon has formed. The first of Debussy’s three symphonic sketches gathers motion in successive waves, withdraws, and finally opens into a broad orchestral close. This is Paul Paray’s Detroit orchestral performance, distinct from the band transcription elsewhere in the collection.

sections.label: Dawn · Slow gathering
sections.mNote: A very slow introduction lets instrumental fragments emerge over low sustained sound.

sections.label: A · The sea in motion
sections.mNote: After the opening build, individual themes pass between orchestral sections.

sections.label: B · Renewed motion and retreat
sections.mNote: Renewed energy gives way to quiet before the final broadening.

sections.label: Coda · Toward noon
sections.mNote: Approximate approach to the slow closing chorale and its final expansion.

cues.title: The horizon is still indistinct
cues.text: Debussy begins with a low sustained foundation, soft timpani and harp notes. The first lines emerge gradually rather than arriving as one complete tune. Listen upwards from the bass: the opening’s sparseness makes each new colour count.
cues.evidence: Durand score, printed pp.143–145 (PDF pp.1–3): https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/b/b6/IMSLP15420-Debussy_-_La_Mer_%28orch._score%29.pdf. The report shows a comparatively low opening level and the first larger build around 1:05–1:20; the cue concerns the opening texture.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fragments before a theme
cues.text: Across the introduction, short wind phrases appear above the low background. Follow how a phrase can be answered by another colour without becoming a regular question-and-answer tune. The parts help establish a space before they establish a long melody.
cues.evidence: Durand score pp.144–145 contains cor anglais, trumpet and woodwind fragments above low strings and timpani. The report’s 0:42–0:52 changes are broad anchors, not proof of individual entrances.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Three sketches, one work
cues.text: Debussy calls La Mer three symphonic sketches. Their titles move from dawn to noon, through the play of waves, to a dialogue of wind and sea. They invite images, but the recurring material also binds the movements into a larger musical design.
cues.evidence: Movement titles in the Durand score; Susan Key’s LA Phil programme note describes the symphonic connections: https://www.laphil.com/works/la-mer

cues.title: A surge, then room again
cues.text: The first larger surge has already retreated. The next stretch keeps moving at a lower recorded level, allowing details to register after the opening build. Compare this pattern of growth and release with the much larger arrival still to come.
cues.evidence: Report: relative level rises from −18.3 dB at 1:05 to −9.3 at 1:20, drops to −21.3 at 1:25, and remains lower through 1:55. This is a measured contour, not a named cadence.

cues.title: An orchestra of smaller groups
cues.text: Debussy repeatedly divides the strings, sometimes giving different desks independent lines. Listen for an accompaniment that seems to move inside itself, not just underneath a melody. The orchestra can change density without simply adding a louder tune on top.
cues.evidence: Divided strings appear throughout movement I in the Durand score, including pp.150–156. This general observation is not an exact desk entrance; the report does not separate instruments.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A publisher receives the dedication
cues.text: The score is dedicated to Jacques Durand, Debussy’s publisher. Its printed pages preserve a practical side of this sound world: divided string parts, precise dynamics and changing instrumental combinations turn the sea image into detailed instructions for musicians.
cues.evidence: Dedication and first publication recorded in the IMSLP catalogue https://imslp.org/wiki/La_mer_(Debussy,_Claude); original Durand scoring in the linked full score. The dedication is a work-level fact.

cues.title: The next rise has more weight
cues.text: A new swell gathers across this stretch. Follow its duration as well as its height: the sound becomes stronger over several phrases before falling back. Debussy makes the larger shape out of unequal rises, not a repeated pattern of identical waves.
cues.evidence: Report: level grows around 3:35–4:10, including −9.3 dB at 3:55–4:00 and −6.8 at 4:10, then recedes to about −22 dB at 4:25–4:30.

cues.title: Between the larger swells
cues.text: In the quieter space, keep a sense of motion even when the orchestral weight is reduced. A line or pulse can persist while its surroundings change. Try listening for continuity rather than waiting only for the next loud arrival.
cues.evidence: The report anchors the withdrawal at 4:20–4:30 and a renewed change at 4:36. The listening instruction deliberately does not assign a specific instrument or exact harmonic function.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A wave on the cover
cues.text: Debussy chose an image derived from Hokusai’s Great Wave for La Mer’s first-edition cover. That visual association is real, but it does not make each orchestral gesture a literal illustration of one crest, boat or patch of foam.
cues.evidence: Susan Key, LA Phil programme note, on Debussy’s choice of Hokusai’s image: https://www.laphil.com/works/la-mer. No individual musical event is assigned to the picture.

cues.title: Another crest, another retreat
cues.text: The later middle stretch builds again and then relaxes. Notice how much quieter the music can become after this crest; the final arrival will need room to grow rather than merely continue at the same intensity.
cues.evidence: Report: the 5:35 window is among the loudest, at −5.0 dB; level falls through 5:45–6:00 and reaches a much quieter region around 6:25–6:40.

cues.title: Quiet does not mean motionless
cues.text: As the recorded level falls, keep following the changing lines rather than treating this as a pause between events. Debussy’s small gestures can prepare a large change in scale without announcing that preparation with a new theme.
cues.evidence: The report places a quiet span from about 6:25 to 7:10, including −27.9 dB at 6:30. This invitation concerns that broad region, not a precise instrumental or harmonic event.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Detroit, not the sea
cues.text: This performance was made in Detroit’s Old Orchestra Hall. Mercury’s later label documentation dates the La Mer sessions to 3–4 December 1955; the mono LP transferred here is catalogued as a 1956 issue. Place, session and release describe different stages of one recording.
cues.evidence: Eloquence Mercury Masters vol.1, CD15 recording information: https://www.eloquenceclassics.com/releases-archive/paul-paray-the-mercury-masters-vol-1-1953-1957/; IA MG50101 item metadata supplies the 1956 mono issue. The label’s later stereo release date is not substituted for this LP.

cues.title: A slower, broader closing span
cues.text: Near the close, the score broadens into a slow chorale-like passage. Sustained wind and brass lines sit above flowing harps before the orchestra expands. Compare this measured breadth with the smaller restless gestures that have carried the movement so far.
cues.evidence: Durand score pp.171–173 (PDF29–31), rehearsal14 Très lent. Report: strong change at 7:18 and increasing level through 7:35–7:55 locate the closing region approximately, not its first bar.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Noon has orchestral weight
cues.text: The final expansion supplies the movement’s strongest recorded passage. Listen through the last surge to the decisive release: this is a different kind of ending from simply letting the opening’s soft sound fade away.
cues.evidence: The report’s loudest windows are 7:40–7:55, with a final fall after 8:05. Durand score p.173 ends with full-orchestra chords. No individual final attack is claimed at 8:01.

transitions.title: The low opening releases moving lines
transitions.how: The introduction accumulates sound over its low foundation, then releases the pressure into more mobile phrases. Short figures are passed among winds and divided strings, so the change is one of motion and orchestral distribution rather than an abrupt switch from silence to a tune. The lighter level after the first swell gives those moving lines room to register.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, opening through the early animated paragraphs; report: first rise at 1:05–1:20, fall at 1:25 and novelty peak1:26. This listening landmark does not claim a bar-aligned thematic boundary.

transitions.title: A withdrawal makes room for renewed motion
transitions.how: The preceding rise falls away before the next region gathers energy. Debussy keeps short figures in circulation while changing their weight and register. Hearing the quiet gap as part of the larger phrase makes the later swell feel prepared, rather than like an unrelated burst of volume.
transitions.evidence: Report: low windows at4:25–4:30 followed by a strong novelty peak4:36 and another build in the5:05–5:35 region. The description concerns the audible contour; no specific chord or solo is assigned to4:36.

transitions.title: Quiet motion opens into a broad chorale
transitions.how: After the extended quiet region, Debussy broadens the pace. Sustained lines in winds and brass rise over the harps’ motion; the full orchestra then enlarges the closing gesture. The arrival depends on the contrast between held notes and continuing figures underneath them. What began as small fragments over a low background now carries the weight of a collective statement.
transitions.evidence: Durand score pp.171–173, rehearsal14 Très lent and following crescendo. Report:7:18 novelty peak and rising level to the7:40–7:55 maximum. Approximate passage placement, not exact bar synchronisation.

source.title: Debussy, La Mer · Durand full score, plates D. & F. 6532 / 6838
source.locator: Movement I, printed pp.143–173. Broad score snapshots located against the opening,1:26 and7:18 audio anchors; not a note-by-note activation map.

timeline.note: Low strings, quiet timpani and harp establish the opening; violas enter as the texture grows.
The early introduction passes short phrases between English horn, trumpet and other winds above the low foundation.
The more mobile region distributes its figures among winds, harp and divided strings.
The slow closing chorale brings sustained brass and bassoon lines above flowing harp figures.
Winds, brass, percussion and strings combine in the movement’s final expansion.

composer.epithet: He made a chord’s spacing, a scale’s missing notes and an instrument’s register determine the course of a piece.

composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, outside Paris. Neither parent was a professional musician. His father’s involvement in the Paris Commune brought imprisonment in 1871; through a connection made during that imprisonment, the boy came to the piano teacher Antoinette Mauté, Verlaine’s mother-in-law. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1872, aged ten. Antoine Marmontel trained him as a pianist; Ernest Guiraud later taught him composition. His resistance to harmonic rules developed inside this education: he could play, analyse and compete successfully in the system he came to distrust.

From 1880 he spent summers working for Nadezhda von Meck, Tchaikovsky’s patron, playing chamber music and teaching her children. Travel with her household took him to Italy and Russia. In Paris he accompanied the soprano Marie Vasnier, with whom he had an affair, and wrote songs for her flexible high voice. In their accompaniments, the piano’s register, resonance and passing harmonic changes can supply a second interpretation of the words. The early songs also show how thoroughly he knew the French vocal tradition he would alter.
